Sitting Amongst the winding cobblestone and looming houses of Ghant is the house of knives. You'd never know it from its neighbors. Just either little house on the hill amongst so many other little house.

In this little house, no one lives. Yet the candles remain lit. No one comes or goes, yet there are always new voices heard inside.

Village children, prone to curiosity, take the front door. They find nothing but am empty room, which is most curious considering the candle and voices. Sometimes the room contains trinkets and toys, some children say.

The thief, prone to greed, takes the back. They find coins and gems, not many but more than none. The smart thief returns and again he finds more coin.

The arcanist, prone to power, demands entry by whatever power dwells here. The cellar opens and there he finds a thesis on spatial warping. Satisfied, he goes and studies it.

A distraught and aging mother, prone to compassion, goes to the house seeking balm for her ailing family. Through the window she sees a bundle of herbs. Thankful, she goes and provides relief.

All of them find a knife in their back. This is the House of Knives, and so the price is set.

The house of knives exists as a story within my world, told to children and the greedy as a sort of cautionary tale.

Do you flip things in your life? Buy low and sell high? How's that working out?

For about five years I was buying used guitars and flipping them. I was pretty selective about what I purchased, and the price paid. Generally pocketed anywhere from 50-200% profit on each sale. Helps to know the market, but that required a lot of time spent reading guitar player message boards. Eventually got tired of the effort, the goofball buyers and had amassed a very nice personal collection (for free, essentially) of instruments...so I quit.

I used to do this too! That funded the purchase of the gear I decided to keep. It wasn't really as a primary source of income or anything. I started about 8 years ago and did it for about 4. Crazy the kind of price changes that have happened since then - I still check it out the current market for gear from time to time.

It really was fun like you said getting all this gear basically for free - albeit for a short time. Gave me a good sense of the range of potential of build quality, tones, general coolness and mystique etc possible in different gear. I kind of went crazy at some point and decided I would not just stop flipping but quit music entirely and sold everything I could find a buyer for. The only thing that I couldn't sell was my '62 avri Stratocaster, but I now realize it's the only thing I couldn't have replaced. That guitar is an extension of me and I probably would never recover from losing it.

Right now the only things I'm flipping are used college textbooks. It's actually remarkably easy and anyone with spare money sitting around that's willing to wait long enough can do the same.

So at the beginning of the Fall and Spring semesters (around August or January) the prices of a lot of the more common textbooks skyrockets as demand is high and all college students are buying them up. However if you wait for a month or two, then all these exact same textbooks are going for jackshit compared to these times. A textbook that I sell on Amazon during it's prime might be around $50-$100 but in the middle of the semester that'll typically drop to something like $20-$60.

If you dive really deep into it, you can single out some textbooks that aren't really used by many school that will pretty much only cover the shipping costs. Those have been the true gold mines in my experience because from the student's perspective they're pretty much willing to pay anything short of the ~$200 to get it new. Flipped those for up to 5x what I paid for them.

The USPS also has a "media mail" option which from I've read is the single cheapest way to ship anything. So much so that they actually open some packages to check and make sure it's a textbook because so many people try to abuse that system.

It's the easiest way I've ever made myself some extra beer money.

Also, as someone who almost always takes summer courses, I've noticed this same spike in price in the summer, but it's nowhere near as significant. I'll typically wait to sell the books I uses during the spring semester for when the fall semester begins.
